sentences.text: This bird grew to about two-thirds the size of the modern greater rhea, reaching a height of approximately 90 cm. It possessed a narrow beak similar to tinamous, lithornithids, and cassowaries, along with rather large wings.
The genus Diogenornis was described in 1983 by Brazilian scientist Herculano Marcos Ferraz de Alvarenga from fossils found in the Itaboraí Formation in southeastern Brazil.
The unspecialized traits of Diogenornis suggest it had recently evolved from a flying ancestor.
Diogenornis co-existed with early rheas, indicating very high ratite diversity in South America during the Paleogene.
Diogenornis is classified within the superorder Palaeognathae and the order Casuariiformes.

Although initially classified in the family Opisthodactylidae, further examination showed Diogenornis was more similar to the modern rhea. Recent phylogenetic studies suggest Diogenornis has a closer affiliation to Australian ratites, such as cassowaries and emus.
Diogenornis lived from the Middle Paleocene to the Early Eocene, specifically during the Ypresian, from 56 to 48.07 million years ago.
The presence of Diogenornis expands the known range of this clade to the South American Paleocene, well before the appearance of Emuarius.
